To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

relative initial weight is a strong independent predictor of survival in rats with diethylnitrosoamine-induced hepatocellular carcinoma, that the relative initial weight of the rats was not associated with tumor size or tumor latency, and that the relative initial body weight of rats undergoing transarterial embolization was not associated with survival or tumor size or latency.

1) relative initial weight is a prognostic factor that is associated with improved survival in a translational model of diethylnitrosoamine-induced hepatocellular carcinoma; 2) the effect of relative initial weight on survival is independent of tumor latency and tumor size at diagnosis; 3) relative initial weight does not alter tumor latency; and 4) relative initial weight can be measured by using a simple formula.

relative initial body weight (RW) is associated with improved survival without altering tumor latency in a translational rat model of diethylnitrosoamine (DENA)-induced hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and transarterial embolization (TAE).
